_comment: Hand corrections to the reader's output for A9, in pixels of the
full-resolution crops in .build/a9/ (see imageSize / sheetImageSize).
Positions are box CENTRES, which is what build_coords.py divides by the
image dimensions.
The board read well: 159 of 188 placeable designators, 76 percent, and the
silkscreen stands clear of the component outlines so nothing was fused.
Every one of the 159 was rendered and looked at. All 103 'agreed' and all 12
'single' markers were right; 5 of 12 'ambiguous' and 7 of 14 'collision'
were wrong. The 7 wrong collision partners (C1, C5, C16, CR5, K1, K2, U1)
were replaced by hand and their 7 correct partners (C17, C19, C52, CR3,
K11, K29, U11) promoted so their badge stops warning about a disagreement
that has been settled. 31 designators the reader never found were placed by
hand, and every hand placement was rendered with --proposed and checked
before it landed. The board is now at 188 of 188.
H1 and M4 are dropped rather than moved: a rivet and a shield have no
silkscreen, and the reader had put them on C20's and CR3's labels. Both are
in notOnDrawing with the other 20 mechanical parts.
All 18 test points are hand-placed on the board and on their sheets, as a
matter of course. On the board each box spans the label and the wire-loop
footprint printed directly beneath it -- on this drawing the pad is under
the text rather than beside it, so the two are one target.
The sheets are the usual story: 278 machine reads across four sheets, of
which 143 were wrong and are dropped. Sheet 1 is the worst (46 of 75 wrong)
because it carries the TEST POINT INFORMATION box and the two relay
bottom-view keys, and the reader takes a legend row for the thing it names:
twelve test points arrived pointing at their own legend entry, and seven
K-numbers at the bottom-view key captions. Sheet 4 is the opposite case --
its 30 relay coil blocks each carry their own designator legitimately, and
all 30 read correctly. What the reader finds instead of a designator on
these sheets, in order of frequency: a pin number ('16', '15', '8'), a net
or signal name ('OHMS SENSE HI' as H1, 'GROUND PLANE = SCOM' as L6 and Z2),
a value ('11.535K' as Q6, '3.8' as U8), a word from a note ('CARBON' as Z2,
'(MF)' as M4) and a pin-function label ('RESET' as R8, 'IN3' as Q3).
Six markers were reassigned rather than dropped, because the reader had put
one designator's marker squarely on another real designator's label and the
second designator had no marker of its own: sh2 K5 -> K9, sh3 CR5 -> CR9,
Photograph alignment is approximate and the credit says so. Fifteen landmark
pairs: fourteen test point pads along the top edge, where the drawing's
label and the board's silkscreen coincide, and eleven component bodies and
one block of silkscreen text spread over the rest of the board. Residuals
against those pairs are a median of 12 photo pixels and a p90 of 23, which
is about 14 and 26 drawing pixels -- good enough to overlay, not good enough
to measure with. Two things hold it back and both are properties of this
board rather than of the solve. The relay and DIP bodies stand several
millimetres proud, so they carry parallax; and the designator TEXT cannot be
used as a landmark here at all, because Fluke centred it inside the part
outline on the drawing and printed it below the part on the board -- the
K-relay labels sit 100 drawing pixels apart between the two images. Only the
test point row and 'OHMS CAL ASSY' are printed in the same place in both.
